BEHIND THE TRICK · SPOILERS AHEAD

The room was fictional.
The missing difference wasn’t.

You changed the question you asked the experiment. That revealed something the first measurement could not.

This is a short introduction to quantum coherence: a relationship between the parts of a quantum superposition that lets their contributions reinforce or cancel. The room uses a precise, ideal four-qubit example. It does not simulate ghosts, real lantern hardware or a whole quantum computer.

First, what did those four marks mean?

A qubit is a quantum system with two possible outcomes for a chosen measurement. We label a dark mark 0 and a lit mark 1. A row such as 1011 is the result of measuring four qubits: three lit marks, so an odd count.

Every trial prepares a fresh system. We are not repeatedly interrogating the same four particles, and the machines do not react to being watched by a person. The “lens” is a story device for choosing a different measurement procedure.

Two recipes. One identical view.

The mixture chooses between two complete preparations at random: all four zero or all four one, with equal probability. The other machine prepares a superposition of those alternatives with a particular relative minus sign. That sign is part of how the alternatives combine; it is not a negative probability.

Through the ordinary lens, called Z measurement, both recipes give 0000 or 1111, each with a 50% chance. Taking more Z samples does not uncover the sign. Even perfectly matching Z charts would not tell the recipes apart.

What does turning the lens do?

The turned lens represents X measurement on every qubit. Here the labels 0 and 1 stand for the +1 and −1 outcomes of X, not the same property measured by Z. In this procedure, both alternatives contribute to each possible four-mark result.

For the specified quantum recipe, we add those contributions before calculating a probability. For an even number of lit marks, the contributions point in opposite directions and cancel. For an odd number, they reinforce. This is interference.

⟶+⟵= 0

For the random mixture, the alternatives do not interfere with one another. We average their probabilities. Both even and odd counts remain possible.

PreparationOrdinary / ZTurned / X
Specified quantum state0000 or 1111 equallyOdd count only
Random mixture0000 or 1111 equallyEven or odd, equally likely

Why the keeper’s promise matters

The note promises exactly one of each recipe. An even X row is impossible for the specified ideal quantum state, so it excludes that machine. The other machine is identified using the keeper’s promise.

An all-odd sample alone is not a proof of arbitrary quantum coherence or entanglement. A mixture can produce all odd results by chance: for 16 independent trials, the probability is 1 in 65,536. If neither machine produces an even row, the game asks you to test again instead of rewarding a guess.

In real hardware, noise and imperfect measurements require statistical analysis. This game has no such noise. It is a two-candidate teaching puzzle, not a general quantum certification protocol or a new research result. Different coherent states can have different X patterns: a plus sign instead of minus makes this example even-only.

The algebra, when you want it

The quantum state is the four-qubit GHZ-minus state:

|ψ⟩ = (|0000⟩ − |1111⟩) / √2

For a result with k lit marks in X, its amplitude is

a(k) = [1 − (−1)k] / (4√2).

Even k gives zero. Odd k gives amplitude 1/(2√2), so probability 1/8 for each of the eight odd strings. The mixture gives probability 1/16 for every string. Its density matrix has the same Z-diagonal entries as |ψ⟩, but lacks the off-diagonal terms linking 0000 and 1111. Coherence is defined relative to a basis; here the preparation comparison is relative to Z.

Run the experiment yourself

You only need Python. Download the standalone experiment, then run:

python3 learn_measurement.py

It calculates probabilities from amplitudes, compares the mixture and samples measurements. Change the relative sign and predict what happens before running it again. The longer walkthrough introduces each step. The game's samples come from the same checked Python reference; its cards are observations, not scripted outcomes.

Sources and further reading

These sources explain the underlying ideas. They are not endorsements of the game. Reviewed 30 October 2026.

  1. Greenberger, Horne & Zeilinger, “Going Beyond Bell’s Theorem”. Original 1989 chapter, electronic version 2007. Historical source for GHZ states and multipartite quantum correlations. Our puzzle is not a Bell test.
  2. Baumgratz, Cramer & Plenio, “Quantifying Coherence”. Physical Review Letters 113, 140401 (2014), arXiv v3. A rigorous resource-theory treatment of coherence. The game illustrates interference; it does not estimate a coherence measure.
  3. IBM Quantum Learning: quantum information in multiple systems. A more formal introduction to multi-qubit states and measurement probabilities.

About the room

I studied physics at Brown and wanted to return to the strange question at the heart of this experiment: how can two preparations look identical until you change the measurement? This Halloween room is one way to explore it.

Atmospheric discovery was inspired by Inscryption and Ethan Mollick’s WONTFIX. The room, story and procedural sound here are original. Three.js supplies the 3D renderer under its MIT license. No models run during play, and no account is required.
